questions.prompt: Prove or disprove: the sum of any three consecutive integers is divisible by 3. Your response should present a complete mathematical argument and evaluate whether the claim generalises to any n consecutive integers.

levels.title: Level 3 (High Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Comprehensive, accurate technical knowledge using correct terminology throughout.
levels.ao2: Thorough application to the scenario with coherent, logical progression of ideas.
levels.ao3: Critical, balanced evaluation; arguments substantiated and a reasoned conclusion drawn.

levels.title: Level 2 (Medium Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Sound knowledge of concepts with mostly correct terminology.
levels.ao2: Application to the context is present but uneven or partially developed.
levels.ao3: Some evaluation; arguments one-sided or conclusions asserted rather than reasoned.

levels.title: Level 1 (Low Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Basic knowledge; isolated facts or terminology with occasional inaccuracy.
levels.ao2: Superficial or generic application; little reference to the actual scenario.
levels.ao3: Little or no evaluation; opinion without justification.

indicativeContent: Algebraic representation n + (n+1) + (n+2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n+1) — constructive proof
Recognition that the factorised form proves divisibility for all integers n
Generalisation: sum of k consecutive integers is kn + k(k-1)/2
Divisibility by k holds when k is odd; fails for even k — counterexample needed
A counterexample for even case e.g. 1+2=3 not divisible by 2
Logical structure: claim, proof, generalisation hypothesis, verdict with justification

indicativeContent: Correct interpretation of p=0.04: probability of such data (or more extreme) if no real effect
p does NOT measure the probability the technique works

Multiple-comparison and replication concerns honestly raised

questions.prompt: A student models a basketball free throw as a projectile moving under gravity alone. Discuss the assumptions built into this model, evaluate which are most questionable for a basketball, and explain how refining the model would change the predicted motion.

levels.title: Level 3 (High Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Comprehensive accurate knowledge: systematic treatment prioritising air resistance with correct qualitative refinements.
levels.ao2: Fully sustained, logically structured application to the scenario.
levels.ao3: Balanced, well-justified evaluation reaching a supported conclusion.

levels.title: Level 2 (Medium Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Sound knowledge: identifies several standard assumptions with sound evaluation of at least one.
levels.ao2: Applies the physics to the scenario with mostly coherent reasoning.
levels.ao3: Some evaluation, though uneven or incomplete.

levels.title: Level 1 (Low Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Limited accurate knowledge: lists an assumption without analysis.

indicativeContent: Standard assumptions: projectile is a particle, gravity constant, no air resistance, no wind, no spin effects
Basketball is light with large cross-section — air resistance is significant relative to its weight, the most questionable assumption
Drag reduces range and maximum height; the optimal launch angle drops below 45°
Constant g is excellent over a few metres; the particle assumption ignores spin but the Magnus effect is small for a gentle free throw
Refinement cost: drag models destroy closed-form solutions, requiring numerical methods — accuracy bought with complexity

questions.prompt: A student uses the Newton–Raphson method to solve x³ − 2x + 2 = 0, starting from x₀ = 0. The iteration fails to converge. Analyse why numerical root-finding methods can fail, using this example and others, and evaluate strategies for choosing methods and starting values that make failure less likely.

levels.title: Level 3 (High Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Comprehensive accurate knowledge: precise analysis of failure mechanisms with evaluation of mitigation strategies.
levels.ao2: Fully sustained, logically structured application to the scenario.
levels.ao3: Balanced, well-justified evaluation reaching a supported conclusion.

levels.title: Level 2 (Medium Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Sound knowledge: identifies genuine failure modes with correct reference to the example.
levels.ao2: Applies the physics to the scenario with mostly coherent reasoning.
levels.ao3: Some evaluation, though uneven or incomplete.

levels.title: Level 1 (Low Mark Band)
levels.ao1: Limited accurate knowledge: states failure can happen without mathematical reasons.

indicativeContent: x₀ = 0 gives x₁ = 1 then x₂ = 0 — the iteration oscillates in a cycle rather than converging (Newton–Raphson can be periodic)
Failure mechanisms: f′(xₙ) ≈ 0 sends xₙ₊₁ far away; cycles; divergence to infinity; convergence to an unintended root
For x³ − 2x + 2 the derivative vanishes at x = ±√(2/3), creating a region where iterates behave erratically
Mitigation: sketch or evaluate f first — a sign change over [a, b] guarantees a root exists there
Bracketing methods such as bisection converge slowly but cannot oscillate — robust when behaviour is unknown
Newton–Raphson converges quadratically near a root when f′ is well-behaved — speed in exchange for fragility
Practical solvers combine methods: bracketing for safety, Newton–Raphson for polish
